articles.title: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
articles.summary: The research points in one direction: If students aren't careful about how they use AI-enabled tools, then academic performance can plummet. It's a huge challenge for teachers.

image.caption: More than 90% of young Germans between the ages of 12 and 19 report using at least one AI applicationImage: Matthias Balk/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.
Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
'Cognitive outsourcing'
In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

blocks.caption: Tablets are commonplace in many high schools and from there, it's just a short click to ask an AI for the answersImage: Hauke-Christian Dittrich/picture alliance

blocks.text: Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.
"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.
Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.
Lower scores, thanks to AI
Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.
Education in transition: How AI is changing teaching

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.
Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.
How to deal with AI in class?
US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.
But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

blocks.caption: German teacher Julian Hinn said he uses AI strategically with older studentsImage: Julian Hinn

blocks.text: Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

Ninety-one percent of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.
The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.
The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.
Students should question AI, too
Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.
"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.
Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.
In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.
"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

blocks.caption: Homework with AI? The temptation is great but teachers say students aren't doing themselves any favorsImage: Max Slovencik/APA/picturedesk.com/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.
But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.
The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.
In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.
Estonia adds AI to the classroom
Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.
It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.
Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
articles.summary: Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools.

Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”.
He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade.

Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer, Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”.
“If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham.

Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s.

Some young people will lose their personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit.

The report will also recommend cutting national insurance paid by businesses over five years for employees aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality. The move could cost as much as £5bn, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank.
The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year.

Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it.

Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront.

Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.”

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently.

He said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work.

blocks.caption: The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, told the BBC that benefit changes were necessary. Photograph: Jeff Overs/PA

blocks.text: But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said.

“You will actually get more than you will now. He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs, and for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work.

Change was necessary, he added, because the number of young people claiming personal independence payments (Pip) had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had increased by 80%.

Burnham hit out at the Conservatives and Reform, who have called for deep and immediate cuts to welfare, with Kemi Badenoch vowing to slash the bill by £36.1bn by 2030 if the party wins the next general election.
after newsletter promotion

Under the plans 70% of child benefit disability-related claims linked to ADHD and “milder” behavioural disorders and learning disabilities would be cut, with Labour calling the proposals “a charter for human misery”.
The shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, acknowledged the plans could mean around half a million children losing disability-related payments.

“This is to help those children,” she told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, adding that under the plans, child mental health services would receive £1bn of funding. “The point of that funding is because there are children who are struggling. Let’s use this funding in the best possible way to support those children.”

Burnham accused past Conservative governments of taking “a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt” of austerity cuts. “What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again,” he said.

“The crude cuts they are proposing … would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services.”
A survey of young people by the Children’s Commissioner, which received more than 1m responses, found that more than half said they were worried about getting a good john in the future.
The responses revealed that the UK’s young people want to work but face “huge challenges” finding experience and opportunities, said Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England.
“The message is clear. Young people are ambitious, they want to work, they want a good job,” she said.
“We need to help them get the skills, the experience and opportunities to find work.

“They need a full, rich education that gives them the knowledge and skills to get on in life, but too many are being let down by the advice and careers support they receive, which many young people do not feel isn’t good enough.”
Responding to the survey, Milburn said he had not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet while writing the review.
“All too often the system – from health to welfare to the labour market – has failed them. That’s why a fundamental system reset is needed to give hope back to young people,” he said.

articles.title: SC scraps bond rule for seafarers claiming disputed awards
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional and void the requirement for seafarers to post a bond before claiming disputed monetary awards and damages pending appeal or judicial review.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 3:38pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional and void the requirement for seafarers to post a bond before claiming disputed monetary awards and damages pending appeal or judicial review.

In a press release issued Monday, the SC En Banc partially granted five consolidated petitions filed by seafarers, labor groups and maritime schools questioning provisions of Republic Act No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, as well as its implementing rules and related issuances.

Under Section 59 of the law, monetary awards for wages, statutory benefits and undisputed amounts were immediately executory. However, seafarers were required to post a bond before claiming disputed amounts and damages to guarantee repayment if the ruling was later overturned or modified.

The SC ruled that the bond requirement violated the constitutional guarantees of due process and equal protection by imposing a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments, a requirement not similarly imposed on other workers.

“The Court held that the bond requirement violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Constitution. It imposed a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments and subjected them to a disadvantage not similarly imposed on other workers,” the SC said.

“While recognizing the State’s interest in preventing ambulance chasing and protecting the maritime industry against unrestituted awards, the Court found that these objectives did not justify the challenged restriction on the execution of monetary awards,” it added.
Section 59 also allowed the Department of Migrant Workers’ Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan (AKSYON) Fund to cover the bond premiums.

The SC likewise declared this provision unconstitutional, saying the use of public funds to pay private bond premiums violated Section 29(1), Article VI of the Constitution, which requires public money to be spent strictly for a public purpose.
The High Court also struck down provisions of Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Department Order No. 247, Series of 2025, that enforced the bond requirement.
The SC emphasized, however, that the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void.
“The law therefore remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void,” it said.
Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh penned the decision. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Mozambique's justice under scrutiny as Venancio Mondlane faces trial
articles.summary: The trial of opposition politician Venancio Mondlane begins in Mozambique on Tuesday. The former presidential candidate is facing five charges, including incitement to terrorism.

image.caption: After parliamentary and presidential elections in November 2024, supporters of opposition politician Venancio Mondlane took to the streetsImage: ALFREDO ZUNIGA/AFP

blocks.text: The trial of Venancio Mondlane will shape the political future of Mozambique, and influence how much trust citizens place in state institutions.

From November 17, the country will be watching the opposition politician and former presidential candidate as he faces five counts, including publicly advocating crimes and inciting collective disobedience and terrorism after the October 2024 elections.
If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 20 years in jail.
'Nothing to do with violence'
Mondlane has denied all the charges, and said he never called for violence. In fact, he said, his public statements were meant to prevent violence.

"I have more than enough evidence that numerous statements I made went in exactly the opposite direction," he told DW during a Septembervisit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg. "I have more than sufficient evidence that numerous statements I made were in exactly the opposite direction."
'Nothing can prove that I am the one who promoted violence'

The post-election protests had two main goals: To pressure authorities to investigate extrajudicial killings of members of Mondlane's political movement, and to find out the truth about election results.
"These were the fundamental issues of our entire protest," he said. "This has absolutely nothing to do with violence."
Where does criminal incitement begin?

In the October 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections, Mondlane ran as a presidential candidate with the support of the left-wing opposition party Podemos. Afterwards, he did not recognize the official election results.

blocks.caption: Demonstrations in Mozambique continued for weeks after the October 2024 electionsImage: Jaime Álvaro/DW

blocks.text: The election saw Daniel Chapo of the Frelimo party declared winner. Frelimo has governed Mozambique since independence in 1975.

After the elections were called, Mondlane and his supporters protested. For months, there were demonstrations, strikes and road blockades as well as violent clashes with security forces nationwide. According to reports from civil society groups, more than 400 people died. Shops and public facilities were looted or destroyed.

The public prosecutor's office has alleged a connection between Mondlane's public calls to action and the violence. The indictment is based on his live broadcasts on social media, in which he called for protests, strikes and civil disobedience.
Albino Forquilha, who heads Podemos and is Mondlane's former political ally, is expected to testify at the trial. However, he told DW that he would not appear as a witness for the prosecution.

Forquilha said he would report his own observations of the protests and would only testify to what he personally experienced. He cannot predict whether his statements will benefit Mondlane or the state.
Prosecution overstating some aspects, says critic
Baltazar Fael, a prominent Mozambican lawyer, argues that the prosecution's case is problematic.

Speaking with DW, he warned against equating indictment with conviction. "What we currently have is an indictment by the public prosecutor," he argued. "And this does not mean that the accused has already been convicted."
The court will hear arguments from both sides and must decide whether what happened constitutes a criminal offense. Predicting the outcome is difficult.

blocks.caption: Lawyer Baltazar Fael says he has doubts about the trialImage: Silaide Mutemba/DW

blocks.text: Fael is particularly critical about the charge of incitement to terrorism. For this charge to be valid, a plausible connection between Mondlane's statements and specific acts must be proven. Acts of violence that occurred following his calls to action will not be enough to convict him on this charge, Fael said.

The question is whether Mondlane actually intended to incite terrorist acts. "What power did Venancio Mondlane actually have to incite people to commit all these crimes?" Fael asked, adding that, after reading the indictment, he believes the prosecution is overstating some aspects of its case.
Is the case politically motivated?
There are also questions as to whether the trial might be politically motivated in some way. For years, Mozambique's justice system has been criticized because of potential political interference.
Fael said several factors have raised doubts. "The timing of the trial and the circumstances that led to it — namely, a challenge to the election results — are clearly political in nature," he said.
Additionally, the speed at which the trial was prepared might also give the impression that there's some political pressure at work here, he added.
What an opposition leader's trial means for Mozambique

Adelino Muchanga, chief justice of Mozambique, has emphasized that his court will decide the case based on facts. But observers are still asking how independent the judiciary can be when the defendant is one of the most prominent critics of Mozambique's political leadership.

The Supreme Court's decision not to allow a live broadcast of the trial has drawn further criticism. Mondlane's defense requested a live broadcast but was denied by the court, which reasoned that such a broadcast could endanger the safety of those involved, influence or intimidate witnesses and disrupt proper conduct of the trial.

Critics see this refusal as a setback for transparency, especially since another recent, prominent trial, the so-called "hidden debt scandal" where state-owned companies secretly borrowed billions from international banks, got extensive media coverage.
Social unrest remains
Additionally, the causes of the protests that sparked this trial have not disappeared. DW's interviews with citizens in the northern Mozambican city of Nampula make this clear.
"The people still want the same thing," one resident told DW. "They wanted Venancio to become president."
Another Nampula resident pointed out that "the population protested against hunger and the lack of jobs for young people. And that's legitimate."

Still, some in Nampula just want to see closure, preferring to have peace and an end to the demonstrations. Even if the economic situation could be better, the country has to return to normality at some stage, they argued.
Additional reporting by Amos Fernando and Conceicao Matende in Maputo.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go
articles.summary: The Rockwell sale accomplishes something months of Lopez family boardroom battles couldn't

blocks.text: Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles
Federico “Piki” Lopez is selling a business that is making money. And the buyer is his cousin Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, one of the loudest critics of his leadership.

Rockwell Land, the property developer behind Power Plant Mall and Alabang Town Center, earned about P3.79 billion in profit in the first nine months of 2026, up 21.5% from a year earlier. Yet on November 12, the board of First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), chaired by Piki, approved selling its controlling stake in Rockwell to Crème Investment Corporation, the private holding firm of Gabby and siblings, for P15.92 billion.
A company doesn’t have to be failing to be sold. Sometimes the controlling owner simply wants to put the money somewhere else.

In Piki’s case, the decision also follows months of open warfare among the third-generation Lopez cousins over who should run the family empire. Last year, First Gen sold control of its natural gas business to Prime Infrastructure in a deal worth about P48.8 billion. This year, it rejected an Indonesian investor’s offer valuing geothermal producer Energy Development Corporation (EDC) at US$5 billion. Meanwhile, FPH has spent billions buying back its own shares while keeping regular dividends flat.
Piki is keeping the energy business a foreign buyer wants, while letting go of a profitable developer his cousins want to own.

The sale solves two problems at once: it hands FPH extra cash for capital-hungry power projects, and it moves Rockwell, long tied to the late Manuel “Manolo” Lopez and his children, out of Piki’s corporate structure. Still, FPH has public shareholders who didn’t sign up to fund a family truce. For them, the only question that matters is whether selling Rockwell makes financial sense, no matter what it fixes among the cousins.
Rockwell and FPH’s power businesses have very different timelines, but both eat up huge amounts of money.

Rockwell’s P21.6-billion purchase of Alabang Commercial Corporation comes with installment payments running through December 2027, and its project spending hit roughly P9.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Meanwhile, First Gen and EDC are pouring billions into geothermal drilling, renewable energy, battery storage, and hydropower. First Gen’s Wawa and Pakil pumped-storage projects require heavy funding through 2029, with commercial operations targeted around 2030 and big profits expected starting in 2031.

As First Gen President and COO Giles Puno told shareholders in May 2026, “Beginning in 2031, these facilities are projected to contribute approximately P16 billion annually to First Gen’s bottom line, through a 20-year contracted agreement under the Department of Energy’s Green Energy Auction Program.” That is a massive future income stream. But it requires billions in investment years before the cash rolls in. (READ: From ‘king’ to ‘steward’: How Piki Lopez answered the Lopez family rift question)

Pumped-storage facilities use electricity to pump water uphill when power is cheap, then release it to generate electricity when demand spikes. They help stabilize a power grid relying more on renewables, but they are expensive and slow to build. Geothermal exploration is risky, too: companies must spend heavily to drill for underground steam before knowing how much power a site can actually produce.

blocks.caption: Diagram of the 1400 MW Pakil Pumped-storage Hydroelectric Power Project in Pakil, Laguna. Image from Ahunan Power Environmental Impact Statement

blocks.text: Piki has repeatedly built his strategy around the long-term payoff of patient bets, preaching “direction over speed” in his 2026 speeches. In the power business, patience isn’t optional. Selling Rockwell removes one hungry business competing for cash while giving FPH money to spend elsewhere.

The deal also clears Rockwell’s debt off FPH’s combined balance sheet once the developer is no longer a subsidiary. Rockwell carried more than P52 billion in total debt. Still, moving debt off the books isn’t the same as paying it off. And FPH is also giving up Rockwell’s entire property business, including its future earnings and obligations, for cash.

Piki’s strategy becomes much clearer when compared against two energy offers he turned down this year. In July, Barito Renewables Energy, linked to Indonesian billionaire Prajogo Pangestu, made an unsolicited offer valuing EDC’s equity at about US$5 billion (and up to US$7 billion including debt). First Gen said no. In September, its officials said they had no plans to sell EDC. Instead, in September, EDC teamed up with Indonesia’s Sinar Mas group to export its geothermal drilling know-how into Indonesia.

A month after Barito’s approach, parent company FPH also rejected a proposal from global private equity firm KKR to buy more shares in First Gen at P35 per share, a deal that would have handed FPH roughly P10.6 billion in cash. But KKR’s offer came with strings attached. Not just one, but three: it wanted FPH to sell shares at a discount while delisting First Gen from the stock exchange; it would have reduced FPH’s common stake before 50% while lifting KKR to roughly 40% under a new shareholders agreement; and it demanded strict tripwire requiring a mandatory buyout if control ever shifted at First Gen or any holding company above it. FPH said no again, arguing that P35 per share did “not reflect the company’s true value.” Sure enough, weeks later, KKR sold its First Gen stake to Singapore-based Gateway Partners’ Angana finance at P36 per share.

blocks.caption: Making sense of US firm KKR’s offer on Lopez family’s First Gen

blocks.text: Put those numbers side by side and the logic of the Rockwell sale becomes crystal clear. FPH refused to surrender EDC’s irreplaceable geothermal edge at any price, and refused to sell a slice of First Gen at a discount with governances strings attached. By selling Rockwell instead, FPH brings in P15.92 billion, roughly 50% more cash than KKR’s offer without giving up a single share of its core power business or handling an outside partner veto power over the group.

EDC isn’t just a collection of power plants. It owns steam fields, holds development rights, and has spent decades mastering how to find and manage underground geothermal energy. That kind of expertise is hard and expensive to copy. Keeping EDC protects both a steady business and specialized knowledge that can fuel expansion outside the Philippines.

blocks.caption: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target

blocks.text: Rockwell is a different story. Its luxury condos, office leases, and malls make good money, but they sit outside the power and industrial core that increasingly defines FPH. That doesn’t make real estate less valuable. It just shows Piki values geothermal know-how more than owning malls and condos. For EDC, knowledge is worth more kept than sold. For Rockwell, FPH found its price.

FPH isn’t selling Rockwell because it is desperate for cash. In 2025, FPH reported roughly P19.8 billion in net income, including P15.1 billion in recurring profit. First Gen’s natural gas deal also brought major resources into the group (though that P48.8-billion deal value isn’t all sitting around as spendable cash). FPH already holds roughly P76 billion in consolidated cash and short-term financial assets. It also has P38.2 billion in appropriated retained earnings through December 2027—money earmarked for specific company plans, rather than a separate pile of spare cash.

The Rockwell sale will bring FPH P15.92 billion in gross proceeds once it closes. Management hasn’t earmarked it for any specific power project yet. Even so, it gives the company more breathing room to fund investments, pay down debt, or reward shareholders. It could also give FPH room to clean up its messy cross-ownership setup. Lopez Holdings owns 60.67% of FPH, while FPH owns 15.76% of Lopez Holdings, a loop that complicates how dividends flow between the two listed firms, though no plan to untangle it has been announced.

There is another practical perk to selling Rockwell instead of shaking up FPH or First Gen. Big ownership changes at the top companies can trigger expensive penalty clauses in loan and joint-venture contracts—including agreements with Prime Infrastructure and FPH’s lenders. Selling a subsidiary like Rockwell avoids setting off those costly triggers.

blocks.caption: Why everyone wants a piece of the Lopez group’s Energy Development Corp.

blocks.text: How FPH spends its money reveals a lot about Piki’s playbook. In 2025, FPH spent roughly P3.36 billion buying back its own shares, bringing total buybacks to about P13.11 billion by year-end. It later added another P5 billion to the buyback budget through September 2028.
Buybacks and dividends reward shareholders in very different ways:

items: Dividends hand cash directly to every stockholder based on how many shares they own.
Buybacks pay cash only to investors who sell their shares, which shrinks the share count and leaves remaining owners with a bigger slice of the company.

blocks.text: For the Lopez family, which already controls the holding company, ongoing buybacks quietly increase their ownership percentage as long as they don’t sell.

Meanwhile, FPH has kept its regular dividend frozen at P2.20 per share for five straight years, despite strong profits and big asset sales. First Gen even cut its annual dividend from P0.90 per share in 2024 to P0.80 in 2025, citing heavy capital spending and debt payments.

Holding onto cash gives management fuel for massive power projects. But it also puts pressure on Piki to prove that keeping the money beats handing it to investors. With another P15.92 billion coming in from Rockwell, shareholders will be asking: Will this cash go toward more buybacks, new power plants, debt cuts, or finally a bigger dividend?

FPH agreed to sell 5.3 billion Rockwell common shares (about 86.58% of the common stock) at P3 each, plus 2.75 billion voting preferred shares at P0.01 each. That brings the total price to roughly P15.92 billion and transfers 90.74% of the voting power.

In its November 13 disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange, FPH said it engaged BDO Capital & Investment Corporation which valued Rockwell’s common shares at P2.47 to P3.09 per share. The agreed price of P3 falls toward the upper end of that range. FPH said the price was determined through arm’s-length negotiations with Crème. That is a solid benchmark, though it doesn’t automatically prove FPH got the best price for a growing commercial developer.

Rockwell carries heavy debt, construction bills, and unpaid installments from its Alabang deal, all of which weigh on its price tag. On the flip side, it brings steady mall rent, a strong housing pipeline, and prime land. The real question is whether P15.92 billion fairly pays FPH for giving up all those future profits.

FPH noted that the deal was backed by BDO Capital’s independent valuation, reviewed by outside lawyers and independent directors, and still requires regulatory sign-off—including clearance from the Philippine Competition Commission and a mandatory buyout offer for Rockwell’s remaining public stockholders. Those guardrails matter, but investors still deserve to see how the price was negotiated and whether other buyers were ever considered.

The Rockwell sale accomplishes something months of boardroom battles couldn’t: it moves a business tied to Piki’s critics out of the empire he runs. Gabby Lopez and Manolo Lopez’s children challenged Piki’s leadership earlier this year. In September, Piki locked down control of the Lopez Holdings and FPH boards. Now, Gabby’s firm is buying Rockwell, the company long associated with Manolo’s side of the family. (READ: How to make yourself very expensive to fire: The Lopez cousins’ war)

Selling Rockwell could cool down future fights over management, dividends, and spending priorities. It also removes one of Piki’s loudest critics from FPH’s property business. Still, it doesn’t prove that Gabby has been silenced, that the cousins have buried the hatchet, or that the deal is part of a secret peace treaty.

For everyday public stockholders, the bigger issue is whether the deal was cut on fair terms. FPH noted that BDO Capital provided an independent valuation, and that independent directors and outside lawyers were involved. Even so, shareholders still deserve to know how the price was set, how conflicts of interest were handled, and whether FPH considered other buyers.
A deal that calms a family feud can certainly be good for business. But keeping peace in the family isn’t a good enough reason on its own for a public company to sell a profitable subsidiary.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] How the Lopezes got, then lost CBK to the Aboitiz group

blocks.text: Look at Piki’s moves over the past two years and a clear pattern emerges: First Gen sold control of its gas business, turned down a multibillion-dollar offer for EDC, and kept pouring money into renewable energy. FPH spent billions buying back shares while keeping regular dividends flat. Now, it is selling Rockwell for nearly P16 billion.

These deals leave Piki running a conglomerate focused heavily on power and industry, while Gabby’s branch walks away with a profitable property developer outside Piki’s reach. It may be a practical way to separate the cousins’ turf after months of fighting. At the same time, FPH is giving up a proven business with steady cash flow, prime properties, and strong future growth.

There is an argument for selling Rockwell that goes beyond the P15.92-billion price tag. Months of boardroom battles have eaten up time and energy that could have gone into running and growing the business. If the sale lets the cousins pursue their own goals without fighting over the same companies, Piki gains something valuable: the freedom to focus on his power and industrial businesses with fewer distractions and less uncertainty at the top. That kind of peace is hard to price, yet it can make a real difference to how a company runs.

There is an equally strong case for keeping Rockwell. It makes money, owns prime real estate, and could keep sending profits and dividends to FPH for years, cash that could help fund the group’s power projects without giving up a company that took decades to build. Selling Rockwell means trading all those future earnings for a fixed payout today. And while the cash is guaranteed, the peace isn’t. The cousins haven’t announced a formal settlement, and this deal won’t automatically end their disagreements.

Is peace worth it? That comes down to what FPH gains by letting Rockwell go versus what it loses by walking away. Keeping Rockwell brings steady profits and long-term upside. Selling it brings immediate cash, a tighter business focus, and a chance to end a costly family war. Both paths have real value, and both carry risks.

For Piki, the choice isn’t simply between peace and profit. It is a choice between two different futures for FPH: keeping Rockwell inside a diversified empire to generate steady cash alongside its power plants, or concentrating everything on energy and industry while the cousins go their separate ways.
The real question isn’t just whether peace is worth the price of Rockwell. It is whether FPH and its shareholders will be better off with Rockwell—or without it. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: PNP ready to assist in Quiboloy's possible extradition to US
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it is ready to assist in the possible extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) leader Pastor Apollo Quiboloy to the United States should a…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 3:30pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it is ready to assist in the possible extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) leader Pastor Apollo Quiboloy to the United States should a court issue an order for police assistance.

“We will only follow lawful orders from competent courts. If they will include us at meron po silang kautusan na ibigay sa atin,” PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said at a press briefing.
(We will only follow lawful orders from competent courts. If they will include us and they have an order to give us.)
“Whether it's to assist in the transfer and to secure the person of pastor sa pagpunta po sa airport or otherwise very much ready po ang inyong PNP to assist and to render assistance,” he added.
(Whether it's to assist in the transfer and to secure the person of pastor when going to the airport or otherwise your PNP is very much ready to assist and to render assistance," he added.
On November 12, the Makati Regional Trial Court issued an extradition arrest warrant and hold-departure order for Quiboloy and two of his co-accused, the Department of Justice (DOJ) earlier said.

On behalf of the US government, the DOJ filed an extradition petition on Monday against Quiboloy, Teresita Tolibas Dandan, and Helen Panilag in connection with their charges of international human trafficking, sex trafficking, conspiracy, and bulk cash smuggling.
Quiboloy’s lawyer, Israelito Torreon, said on Nov.13 that his client was not surprised by the extradition petition filed against him and is prepared to face the proceedings in court.

Torreon clarified that he does not represent Quiboloy in the extradition proceedings, noting that his duties are limited to the religious leader's pending criminal cases before the Pasig and Quezon City courts.
He confirmed that Quiboloy has already been notified of the extradition petition, which the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed on Monday on behalf of the United States government.
“Please be informed that Pastor Apollo C. Quiboloy has been informed of the extradition proceedings filed against him,” Torreon said.
“They do not come as a surprise to him. He has expected them, and he is ready to face them in court, through the proper legal process and before the proper forum,” he added. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Teodoro on South China Sea code: I'm not paid to trust an adversary
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday declined to say whether he trusted Beijing to honor a proposed code of conduct (COC) in the South China Sea, saying he could not…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday declined to say whether he trusted Beijing to honor a proposed code of conduct (COC) in the South China Sea, saying he could not rely on the good faith of what he described as an “adversary.”
Asked at the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea whether Beijing would uphold such an agreement, Teodoro said: “I am not paid to rely on the good faith of an adversary.”
“If I rely on the good faith of an adversary in my job as defense secretary, then they might as well find somebody else,” he added.

On Sunday, Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said negotiators had made substantial progress but remained divided on key issues, including the code’s geographic scope, definition of terms and whether it would be legally binding.
She said the parties had reached a provisional agreement on about 80 percent of the draft, up from roughly 50 percent when the Philippines assumed the Asean chairmanship.

The lack of a finalized South China Sea code under the Philippines’ chairship was expected given a series of thorny “milestone issues” that remain difficult to resolve, maritime law expert Jay Batongbacal earlier said.
He had earlier assessed that there was a “big chance” negotiations over the COC would not be concluded this year, as Manila pushed to finalize the binding agreement under its leadership.
“It’s not unexpected, and I think even within the different ministries of the different countries, they also were aware of that possibility. So it’s not surprising,” he told the same forum.

“I would expect that Asean will continue to try to move the process forward next year,” he said, though noting that “the same obstacles will still be there… what you call the milestone issues or threshold issues that… are most difficult to resolve will still be there.”
Asean and China pledged in 2002 to come up with a COC on the South China Sea, a framework that seeks to prevent conflict through diplomatic means but it has remained elusive due to slow progress. /dl

articles.title: Marcos calls for renewed political will, cooperation to achieve SDGs
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Monday called for a renewed political will, stronger partnerships, and evidence-based cooperation to realize the United Nations Sustainable Development…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 3:07pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Monday called for a renewed political will, stronger partnerships, and evidence-based cooperation to realize the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) by 2030.
During the 16th ASEAN-UN Summit, Marcos pointed out that only 36% of the accessible SDG targets “are on track” less than four years away from the 2030 deadline.

“Achieving these goals requires renewed political will, stronger partnerships with the private sector, and cooperation that is evidence-based and responsive to the needs of its members, especially developing countries,” the President said.

Marcos said that through the ASEAN-UN Complementarities Initiative, ASEAN is hoped to substantially contribute to advancing progress in these goals by aligning ASEAN 2045 with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
He likewise welcomed the UN General Assembly’s adoption of the resolution commemorating the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia.
Marcos said that the adoption served as a “reaffirmation of conduct for interstate relations in our region and beyond.”
He also noted the first year of the ASEAN-UN Plan of Action 2026-2030.
“Our cooperation spans peace and security---from combating trafficking in persons, online scams, and illicit drugs, to peacekeeping and keeping Southeast Asia free of nuclear weapons,” Marcos said.

“It extends to trade facilitation, digital transformation, the blue economy, the ASEAN Power Grid, and sustainable minerals development. It also covers health, food, security, disaster management, climate action, and the protection of women, children, persons with disabilities, and science and technology cooperation,” he added.
BARMM polls

Secretary-General António Guterres, on the other hand, congratulated the Philippines for what he described as a “successful conduct” of the first parliamentary polls in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
He said the elections fully consolidated a “remarkable peace process” in the region.
“This should serve as an example well beyond the Philippines and this region,” Guterres said.
UN concerns
The UN chief, however, lamented the impacts of the tensions between Russia and Ukraine, as well as those in the Middle East, Strait of Hormuz, and the Red Sea, on ASEAN.
“I want to reaffirm the unconditional commitment of the United Nations to defend the rights and freedoms of navigation in all situations,” Guterres said.
He also expressed concern over the continuing crisis in Myanmar.

“Human suffering has reached epic proportions. I call on all parties to protect civilians, uphold international law, and allow safe, sustained, and unhindered humanitarian access,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In…

blocks.text: In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.
It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.
Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.

For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.
Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: a plague of locusts in Poland, 1527. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.

“German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”
He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.
“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni said.
The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.
Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: ‘wondrous dragons’ cross the Bavarian sky, 1533. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.
after newsletter promotion

“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”

The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.
“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”

The five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni said.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: five suns  over Leipzig in 1551. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: “Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.

He said he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”
In this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni said.

Till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and said the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”
He said he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.

A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”

articles.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
articles.summary:
Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.

“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”
Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:

items: Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.
It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

blocks.text: “This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”
However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.

He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.
after newsletter promotion
The BBC understands the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place after Brexit.
Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.
“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

articles.title: Ma Wee Tin O’Shortbreid: a journey in search of the real Highlands
articles.summary: Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became…

blocks.text: Growing up in Scotland, our family was one of many who kept their photographs in an old shortbread tin. The lid usually showed a castle beside a loch, a stag, a Highland coo and plenty of tartan. It was always sunny.
Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid is Scots for “my little tin of shortbread”. The title started as a warning to myself: don’t make the Highlands look like a tin of shortbread.
Then, at Eilean Donan Castle, about as biscuit-tin lid as it gets, I photographed a Chinese tourist under a wee umbrella, remaking the view for her own photograph.
The warning became the title.

blocks.caption: Yellow backpacks and trekking poles rest on benches, with Ben Nevis rising behind

items: Yellow backpacks and trekking poles rest on benches, with Ben Nevis rising behind

blocks.text: They were shot to extinction in Britain, the last one in Shetland in 1918. Brought back from Norway in the 1970s. Now they are one of the island’s biggest draws. A bird once shot on sight is part of the sales pitch. The Scotland on the lid promises wilderness and wildlife. The real one comes with binoculars and a long wait.

blocks.caption: (L-R): Isle of Mull. Out of the camper van, looking for white-tailed eagles and a tourist photographs the Scottish Highlands through a coach window.

items: (L-R): Isle of Mull. Out of the camper van, looking for white-tailed eagles and a tourist photographs the Scottish Highlands through a coach window.

blocks.text: One of the buses that leave Edinburgh every morning to do the Highlands in a day. Most of the day is spent on the bus. Glencoe seen through the window of a Heilan coo (Highland cow).

blocks.caption: Glencoe, Highlands. Two women with a geological map. There was a supervolcano here about 420m years ago. In 1909 it became the textbook case for how one collapses. The glaciers finished the job. The forces that shaped Scotland. No, not the English.

items: Glencoe, Highlands. Two women with a geological map. There was a supervolcano here about 420m years ago. In 1909 it became the textbook case for how one collapses. The glaciers finished the job. The forces that shaped Scotland. No, not the English.

blocks.text: Some of that emptiness was made. Highland regiments fought the empire’s wars while the glens were cleared for sheep and sporting estates. The view people come for was somebody’s home.

blocks.caption: Callanish standing stones, Isle of Lewis. They went up 5,000 years ago, older than Stonehenge.

items: Callanish standing stones, Isle of Lewis. They went up 5,000 years ago, older than Stonehenge.

blocks.text: Visitors arrive looking for a Scotland they’ve seen on screens. They come for wilderness and find a queue, a coach park and a wait for somebody to move out of the frame.

blocks.caption: Isle of Skye. Highland cattle, one of the oldest registered breeds in the world, with a herd book going back to 1885. Bred to stand outside all winter without a hat. Even the coos get a souvenir.

items: Isle of Skye. Highland cattle, one of the oldest registered breeds in the world, with a herd book going back to 1885. Bred to stand outside all winter without a hat. Even the coos get a souvenir.

blocks.text: At the famous sites, I kept noticing how many visitors were Chinese and Indian, from countries Britain once ruled, traded with or fought. They were photographing the familiar symbols of old Scotland. This time, Scotland was the attraction, and they were the ones behind the camera.

blocks.caption: Kilt Rock, Isle of Skye. Named because the cliffs look like a pleated kilt. Nobody believes you’ve been to Scotland without a soaking-wet picture.

items: Kilt Rock, Isle of Skye. Named because the cliffs look like a pleated kilt. Nobody believes you’ve been to Scotland without a soaking-wet picture.

blocks.text: Even the weather is for sale. Cool air and rain have become part of the escape. In what felt like London’s hottest summer ever, Londoners drove north to find the cold and wet, though a week of horizontal rain may test the sales pitch.

blocks.caption: Most Highland roads are one-lane wide with passing places. Out on the open hill, there’s often no fence between the sheep and the road. All the way from Frankfurt to give way to a sheep.

items: Most Highland roads are one-lane wide with passing places. Out on the open hill, there’s often no fence between the sheep and the road. All the way from Frankfurt to give way to a sheep.

blocks.text: I’m making these photographs on repeated trips in my camper van: 60 days and 5,000 miles so far, a good part of it stuck behind a motorhome. I’ve been to Skye five times and driven the North Coast 500 (NC500) road in both directions. The project grew out of Weather Permitting, my photographs of Scotland’s ski centres.

Reaching the wilderness usually means driving to it, on the same narrow roads as residents, deliveries, coaches and motorhomes. An empty road makes a good advert. Everyone driving down it makes a different picture.

blocks.caption: Ben Nevis, near Fort William. Scotland has a daily midge forecast, one to five. People swear by Avon Skin So Soft as a repellent. Only the females bite, while the males feed on flowers. When one finds you, she sends for her pals. Tiny, relentless, and missing from the shortbread tin.

The cook’s been at the same pot since 1932.

blocks.caption: The Lonach Highland Gathering. Highland fling. The proper one is danced on the spot, on the balls of the feet, without ever moving off it. The ladies are about to find out what a true Scotsman wears under his kilt.

Carbost is better known for the Talisker distillery up the road but the wood-fired sauna on the shore has become part of the island’s new wellness trail, alongside the cold-water swimmers, the boutique bothies and the queue for the same photo at the Fairy Poo…

Carbost is better known for the Talisker distillery up the road but the wood-fired sauna on the shore has become part of the island’s new wellness trail, alongside the cold-water swimmers, the boutique bothies and the queue for the same photo at the Fairy Pools. One way or another, you’ll warm up.

blocks.caption: Isle of Lewis. Crofters have had the right to cut peat for their own fire since 1886. Not to sell it. Peat grows about a millimetre a year. A winter’s fire takes thousands of years to make and an afternoon to cut. It heats the house and flavours the whisky.

People were still living in them on Lewis until 1974. Now you can book one for the week. The dog hasn’t been offered a room.

blocks.text: Tourism brings work and money. It also needs people who can afford to live close enough to keep the place running. Between No Motorhomes and No More Homes, it’s getting harder for anyone to stay.

blocks.caption: Isle of Benbecula, Outer Hebrides. Eriskay ponies once carried the crofters’ peat and seaweed. By the 1970s, the breed was down to 20 mares and one stallion. The big grey is an Eriskay, bred with a waterproof coat. The wee one is a miniature shetland pony. Had to buy its own.

blocks.caption: Ceannabeinne beach, near Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Nobody on the sand. Everybody on the bend.

items: Ceannabeinne beach, near Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Nobody on the sand. Everybody on the bend.

blocks.text: The NC500 was launched in 2015 to sell 516 miles of empty road. It worked. Camper van life has its own pitch: freedom, independence, a new view every morning. In practice, it depends on ferry bookings, fresh water, waste points and somewhere you’re allowed to stop. Freedom, it turns out, needs a booking reference.

Travelling this way, I’m part of what I’m photographing, on the same roads, ferries and overnight stops as everyone else. The open road can still end at a full layby or a No Motorhomes sign. Passing places become car parks and viewpoints become campsites.

blocks.caption: Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Everybody parks to face the sea. You used to be able to see it from here.

items: Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Everybody parks to face the sea. You used to be able to see it from here.

blocks.caption: Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500, about as far north-west as the mainland goes. Nothing between here and the Atlantic to slow the wind down. The duvet’s making a break for it.

items: Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500, about as far north-west as the mainland goes. Nothing between here and the Atlantic to slow the wind down. The duvet’s making a break for it.

blocks.text: Over July and August one year, about 14,000 motorhomes and nearly 11,000 tents pitched up within five miles of Durness. A few hundred people live there … The NC500 has been a named tourist route for just over a decade. What will it look like in another 10 or 20 years? Part of making these photographs is recording this moment, before we find out.

blocks.caption: Isle of Skye. Two Highlanders. Only one of them’s been on a shortbread tin.

items: Isle of Skye. Two Highlanders. Only one of them’s been on a shortbread tin.

blocks.text: The pictures are about the gap between Scotland as advertised and the place people find. I set out not to photograph the shortbread tin. I kept finding people trying to climb inside it.
Photographs by Dougie Wallace

articles.title: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches
articles.summary:
Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say

UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the…

blocks.text: UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter.
Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say.
They include supplies of O negative, B negative, O positive and RO blood. People of black heritage have also been asked to donate to help the NHS treat people with sickle cell disease.

The health service needs 5,000 donors every day – who either give blood already or are new volunteers – from now until the new year in order to ensure hospitals have enough for patients. That is because blood has a shelf life of 35 days and platelets of just seven days.
Blood service officials want people to fill 150,000 donation appointments over the coming weeks and help boost what they stress are “life-saving supplies” of vital products.
Each donation takes an hour and can help save three lives, they say.
Winter’s cold weather brings two challenges for blood supply agencies. The greater prevalence of colds, coughs and respiratory illnesses such as flu stops people who are unwell from donating.
It can also leave people with long-term conditions, including sickle cell disease and cancer, needing to receive more blood or transfusions of platelets to safeguard their health.

“Right now, as we move into winter, there is an urgent need to boost our life-saving blood, platelet and plasma supplies”, said Gerry Gogarty, the director of blood and plasma supply at NHS Blood and Transplant.

“With patients reliant on regular transfusions, particularly vulnerable to colds and respiratory illnesses, it is vital that we stay well stocked to ensure the blood is always there when it is needed.”

Earlier this month, the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service announced its first amber alert for O blood types. Stocks had dropped to “unprecedented low levels” because of a shortage of donors and greater use of the blood type over recent months, it explained.

blocks.caption: Donated blood has a shelf life of 35 days, and platelets of just seven days. Photograph: NHS Blood and Transplant/PA

blocks.text: Health chiefs also want to ramp up supplies of blood plasma. That is needed to make medicines for people with serious immune conditions, which become harder to manage in winter.
Bigger donation centres in town and city centres offer the most appointments, especially for first-time donors and those with common blood types, Gogarty said.
He asked those who cannot find an appointment immediately to keep checking back to help take up last-minute availability or cancellations.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Karen Davila quote on ‘more thieves’ in Marcos admin taken out of context
articles.summary: The social media posts omitted context showing that Davila was discussing possible public sentiment, not her own personal views

blocks.text: Claim: News anchor Karen Davila stated that there are “more thieves” serving as public officials under the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook user posted a news card bearing a supposed quote by Davila. As of writing, the post has gained 1,900 reactions, 336 comments, and 251 shares.
The quote attributed to Davila reads, “Maraming magnanakaw sa administrasyong ito at hindi kay Sara Duterte, ‘yun ang sinasabi ng survey.”
(There are many thieves in this administration and it’s not [Vice President] Sara Duterte — that’s what the survey says.)

The facts: The quote was not Davila’s personal statement or opinion, contrary to how it was presented in the social media posts. It was part of a longer exchange between Davila and Batangas 2nd District Representative Jinky Luistro, lead prosecutor in Duterte’s impeachment trial, during a November 5 Headstart interview.

While discussing survey ratings in the context of the ongoing impeachment proceedings, Davila referred to Filipinos’ views of the current administration. She cited WR Numero’s October survey, which found that 65% of respondents were dissatisfied with Marcos, compared with 33% for Duterte. She then questioned whether the corruption allegations that surfaced during Duterte’s trial are affecting public perceptions of the Vice President.

Davila told Luistro, “The Filipino people are saying, ‘Mas ayaw namin ng administrasyong ‘to, ‘yung pagpapatakbo ngayon… mas maraming magnanakaw sa administrasyong ito at hindi kay Sara Duterte’ – ‘yon ang sinasabi ng survey. It’s difficult to hear. Mahirap pakinggan ma’am ha, pero the Filipino people have an economic lived experience according to WR Numero that makes them angrier at this administration than Sara Duterte. That is what’s sad.”

(‘We dislike this administration more — the way things are being run right now… there are more thieves in this administration, and it’s not about Sara Duterte’ — that is what the survey says. It’s difficult to hear. It’s difficult to hear, ma’am, but the Filipino people have an economic lived experience according to WR Numero that makes them angrier at this administration than at Sara Duterte. That is what’s sad.)
The social media posts omitted this context showing Davila presenting possible public sentiment, rather than expressing her own personal views.

In response, Luistro said she hoped the public would recognize that the impeachment proceeding does not represent the administration as a whole. She also emphasized that despite political perceptions, an impeachment trial remains a formal legal proceeding grounded in evidence rather than public opinion expressed in surveys.
“Iba yung survey, iba yung impeachment court (A survey is one thing; an impeachment court is another),” she said.

Presidential polls: Duterte has been dominating recent voter preference polls for the 2028 presidential elections. In the same WR Numero October survey, Duterte is ahead in the presidential preference race with 42% of respondents choosing her, followed by Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo at 16%.
The Vice President also led Pulse Asia’s survey conducted from September 17 to 24, garnering 50% of voter preferences, compared with Robredo’s 26%.

Data visualized by Rappler further showed that Duterte is a frontrunner in numerous presidential poll results as of early 2026. However, past elections suggest that being the top contender in pre-election surveys does not guarantee victory.
Previous fact checks: Rappler has debunked numerous claims about survey findings and election results:

items: FACT CHECK: Post shows AI-generated ‘presidential survey’ results
FACT CHECK: Davao City pre-election survey attributed to OCTA Research is fake
FACT CHECK: Local surveys showing Duterte family, others winning, are fake — Pulse Asia

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.
