articles.title: English was the language I built my career in. In Canada, it became something to prove
articles.summary: Anusuya Datta had never given a second thought to knowing English, having always written and spoken in the language. After moving to Saskatchewan, people continually remarked on her English skills,…

image.caption: Anusuya Datta, seen here speaking at an international scientific conference, has had more than a decade of experience breaking down science concepts into plain-spoken English. But as an immigrant arriving in Saskatchewan, she found her skills in English were seen as an accomplishment in and of thems

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·First Person

Anusuya Datta had never given a second thought to knowing English, having always written and spoken in the language. After moving to Saskatchewan, people continually remarked on her English skills, both in complimentary and derogatory ways.
After moving to Canada, people kept reminding me English was my second language
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Nov 15, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
This First Person column is written by Anusuya Datta, a writer and journalist based in Saskatoon. For more information about First Person stories, see the FAQ.
I had only been in Canada for two weeks when I got the question that would follow me around for the next few years.
I’d gone to the pharmacy to ask about medication. The woman behind the counter looked up and said, “You speak very good English.”
By then, I had spent more than 15 years earning my living in English. Now I was being congratulated for successfully asking about a prescription.
“Thank you,” I said.
“Where did you learn it?”
“In India.”
She looked impressed.
I walked out with my prescription and a piece of information: in Canada, my English was an accomplishment.
Anusuya Datta attends a space conference, posing with a therapeutic robot seal proposed as a companion for astronauts on long missions. (Submitted by Anusuya Datta)

I had assumed I was the one immigrating. It turned out there were two of us. My English had done its paperwork. Canada makes you declare your English. That's what the international English language test is for. My English did very well. We both assumed that was the end of it. But someone had forgotten to send Saskatchewan a copy.

English wasn't the first language I learned, I admit. But it was the one I was educated in. I read novels in it and did a master's in it. Nobody in India ever congratulated me on it. It was like having elbows. You don't get complimented on elbows.
Coming face-to-face with assumptions

The pharmacist wasn’t the last. Neighbours told me I spoke English well. Doctors told me. People in shops told me, with the warmth usually reserved for someone who has parallel parked a combine. They were being kind to a newcomer, and I was grateful. I still am.
I said thank you. Every time. You don't hold up the queue to explain English isn't rocket science, and that you have, in fact, explained rocket science in it.
I have an accent when I speak English
Then my English got a job. So did I, at the same tech company in Saskatoon, which was convenient. We were both hired at a junior level. That seemed fair. We were new.

Soon my English was fine-tuning everyone's copy. Colleagues sent me their drafts the way you send a shirt to the dry cleaner, without conversation and expecting it back clean. My English had become the office Wi-Fi. Everyone used it. You don’t promote the Wi-Fi.
Eventually, I brought up a promotion on a call with my boss. I was told it was too soon. I didn't have the necessary experience.
“You need to be patient. These things take time,” he repeated, a little too slowly, as if he were weighing my English comprehension skills.
After the call, I sat for a long time. What my English lacked, I understood, was Canadian experience. It had only the other kind, where you do the work.
A year later, I joined an agriculture-technology company. I imagined data and software. The company sold agricultural chemicals in jugs.

This isn’t an attack on chemicals. Chemicals have had a long and successful career in agriculture. Jugs, for their part, have performed admirably throughout human civilization. But I couldn’t understand how the company involved technology.

The company wanted lots of content, the kind that sounds like the future of food. So I asked what the technology was. In my line of work, this is a standard opening question. It turned out to be a hostile act.
I was given a few words. Innovation. Sustainability. Transformation. None was attached to anything. My job was to expand them. I asked for details. I was told to read up.

So I read everything I could find and came back with questions. The boss came back with more keywords. Then the words started changing their meaning. One week, sustainability was the next big thing. The next, it was “woke.”

Finally, I asked why he was saying the exact opposite of what he’d said the week before. That was when he explained the problem. I wasn't understanding his feedback because English wasn't my first language.

The second half was true. I couldn’t fault his research, but it came a little late. My English had been excellent while it produced adjectives. It developed problems the moment it produced question marks.
“I’ve written for American and European organizations for over 15 years,” I told him. “My English has never been a problem. Until now.”

items: I'm fluent in English, but my accent still feels like a barrier to acceptance

blocks.text: I was angry. Of all the things I expected to have to prove in Canada, my English wasn’t on the list.
I ended up leaving the company. My English came with me. We had been through a lot together.
It’s been more than two years since. The bitterness has aged nicely, like cheddar.

Meanwhile, my English and I went freelance. Not one client told me my English was so good. Or so bad. They asked for a redraft when one was needed and sent more work. I recommend this as a form of compliment. It’s quieter and you can invoice for it.

These days I work for a global company with people in Canada, the U.S. and Europe. People here have opinions, too. They tell me when a piece is great and when I’ve got the technology totally wrong. Not one of them has an opinion about my English. A plumber is judged on the pipes. Nobody asks where the wrench is from. I've never been so happily criticized.
English is still not my first language. It's still doing very well. It even has Canadian experience now.
Thank you for asking.

A journalist based in Saskatoon, Anusuya has a keen interest in connecting technology with sustainability and social causes, and writes for various tech media platforms. She has also delivered guest lectures at the University of British Columbia’s school of journalism on the use of satellite imagery in storytelling.

articles.title: Facing 'uncomfortable' questions, King Charles shows the 'soft power' of the Crown
articles.summary: As with trips to Canada in 2025 and the United States earlier this year, King Charles's recent visit to the Caribbean saw him walking something of a diplomatic tightrope at a politically charged…

image.caption: King Charles greets local residents holding national flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on Nov. 2. (Isabel Infantes/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As King Charles was wrapping up his recent trip to the Caribbean and South America, a palace aide let it be known via news reports that he relishes the "tough parts" of his role as monarch and would keep being used in "politically charged" deployments.

There's little doubt the nine-day sojourn was one of the tougher outings of his four-year reign, shrouded as it was in questions about whether the U.K. should apologize for its role in the transatlantic slave trade and pay reparations.
During the trip that took Charles to Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, he spoke of the "great suffering and injustices of the past" and called the slave trade a "shameful chapter."
No apology emerged, but U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated as the visit was unfolding that he was open to calls for a formal apology, a marked change in British policy on the issue.

Burnham rejected calls for financial reparations. But writing in the Guardian newspaper, he said he wanted to "launch a new drive on debt," which included helping more vulnerable countries "repay over a longer time period and with better ⁠rates."
As with trips to Canada in 2025 and the United States earlier this year, Charles was walking something of a diplomatic tightrope at a politically charged time. There seems to be an emerging pattern.
King Charles addresses 'shameful' history of transatlantic slave trade
"He doesn't seem to shy away from uncomfortable historical questions," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

"By acknowledging them and navigating them, he's showing that these are real questions that matter to people. They can't be ignored. But also there is that tacit acknowledgment that his interest and recognition and engaging in those conversations does not direct policies of the British government."
Charles seems to be good at creating opportunities for dialogue "when a more overt political initiative or intervention would be counterproductive," Vovk said.
"So he really is demonstrating how effective the soft power of the Crown is for Britain's foreign relations."

Those relations were front and centre in the recent trip. Along with the calls for an apology and questions over reparations, there is republican pressure to remove the monarch as head of state in some countries.

Terrence Campbell, parliamentary leader of Guyana’s opposition group A Partnership for National Unity, holds placards during a demonstration demanding a formal British apology and reparations for slavery and colonialism in Georgetown, Guyana, on Oct. 30. (Isabel Infantes/Reuters)

"It was a very difficult, a very challenging visit," Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, said in an interview.

"But he survived it, and survived it far better when you compare with the [2022] visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to the Caribbean [that] attracted a huge amount of criticism in its aftermath, both in terms of how it was planned and how the events took place."
That trip had been seen by some as a bid to shore up ties between Britain and the Commonwealth countries on its itinerary: Belize, Jamaica and the Bahamas.

In the end, that weeklong visit drew more headlines for protests, the republican sentiment fomenting particularly in Jamaica, calls for slavery reparations and uncomfortable moments that seemed more rooted in the colonial past than looking toward the future.

items: What should a royal visit look like? Why William and Kate's recent trip might spark change for future tours

blocks.text: This time, Rowbotham said, Charles made it clear that "as far as he was concerned, it was a matter for the Caribbean communities to make a choice about who should be their head of state."
"He was happy to continue to serve but it was something which he would not fight if they made a different decision."
Charles carried out numerous engagements in the three countries he visited, with many focusing on issues he has made a priority, including the environment and conservation, youth and sustainability.

An Indigenous child, right, presents King Charles, left, with a traditional beaded necklace during a meeting with Indigenous leaders at the National Toshaos Council at Umana Yana on Oct. 30 in Georgetown, Guyana. (Ben Stansall/Getty Images)
Any royal visit has its moments. This one had the umbrella — or initial lack thereof for the King — as the skies opened up in Antigua and Barbuda.
"He was initially clearly taken aback when there was no handy umbrella," Rowbotham said.
"He subsequently laughed it off and simply carried on," she said, calling it "the mark of a monarch who knows how to be diplomatic in a stressful situation."
King Charles gets soaked in Antigua as Camilla gets only umbrella
The moment reminded Vovk of the time Charles got frustrated over a pen holder while signing documents during the ceremony confirming him as monarch in 2022.
"He has certainly gotten better at being able to laugh about those sorts of things."
Remembering the fallen
Queen Camilla, left, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, attend the Remembrance Sunday ceremony at the Cenotaph on Whitehall in central London on Nov. 8. (Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images)
Members of the Royal Family honoured the memory of the fallen at annual events around London in recent days.

King Charles led the tributes on Remembrance Sunday at a ceremony attended by thousands of veterans at the Cenotaph in central London. While Charles, Prince William and others laid wreaths, Queen Camilla, Catherine, Princess of Wales, and others watched from the balcony of a nearby building.
The night before, Charles and Camilla led senior members of the Royal Family for an evening of remembrance at Royal Albert Hall.
Princess Anne, front centre, and Prince William attend the National Service of Remembrance at the Cenotaph on Nov. 8 in London, England. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)
A few days earlier, Birgitte, the Duchess of Gloucester, on behalf of Camilla, opened the 98th Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey.
The remembrance events are a high point of the royal ceremonial year.
The events were little changed from previous years, something that stood out to Vovk.
"This is where ritual culture becomes so important for reinforcing consistency and values across generations," he said.
"It is something that unites the Crown and the people in memory, in grief, in a sense of responsibility."
Birgitte, Duchess of Gloucester, centre, looks on during her visit to the 98th Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey on Nov. 5 in London. (Alberto Pezzali/Getty Images)
Meghan's father cut off monitor days after arrest, officials say

Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was in custody this week after authorities in Florida said he cut off an ankle monitor days after his arrest on allegations of keeping child sexual abuse materials.

Meghan hasn't commented publicly in recent days, and pulled out of a speech she had been planning to give in Belgium on Tuesday. She appeared that day with her husband, Prince Harry, as he spoke at the European Parliament in Brussels.

Earlier, however, Meghan had said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about her father had been sent to London police in 2019.
"I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."
Meghan Markle's father arrested, charged over child sexual abuse images

Media attention for several years has focused on the estrangement, and observers see the possibility recent events could influence public perceptions around Meghan, which have been polarizing in some quarters.

"I'm sure the British public and the wider public, you know, in the States and elsewhere, will have sympathy for her in regards to what's emerged about her father," royal commentator Roya Nikkah told CBC News.
Vovk sees the current situation could "dramatically shift public perception" of Meghan and could "soften public criticism and public reactions" to her.

items: Meghan Markle's father cut off ankle monitor days after arrest, U.S. officials say
Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material

blocks.text: He also wonders if it might help clear the way for some level of rapprochement between Meghan, Harry and the Royal Family.
"I don't know if I'd say a road to reconciliation, but perhaps an opportunity for some mutual support between the Sussexes and the rest of the Royal Family."
The King and the Rocket Man
Elton John, left, and King Charles pose for a photograph at Apple Music Studios, where they were recording John's Rocket Hour, in London, in October. (Apple Music/Reuters)
It's long been known that King Charles has a love of music, particularly of the classical persuasion. But his latest public musings on the overall matter have little royal precedent.
Charles sat down at a microphone opposite Elton John to take part in a special edition of the singer's show.

The episode of Elton John's Rocket Hour aired Saturday — Charles's 78th birthday — on Apple Music. It's intended to celebrate 50 years of the King's Trust — founded by Charles with his navy severance pay as the Prince's Trust in 1976 — and musicians who have supported the youth charity.

"Music has ​always been at the heart of the Prince's, and now the King's Trust," Charles said, adding that the program offered a chance to showcase performers who had supported the charity ​and newer artists it had helped launch.

In a release, Buckingham Palace said the episode also highlights artists — such as the rock band Muse — who received help from the trust at the beginning of their careers, and in some cases went on to support it as alumni.

Muse, which started out in 1994 under the name Rocket Baby Dolls, received a grant from the Prince's Trust to buy sound equipment. In 2018, the band performed a sold-out concert at the Royal Albert Hall in support of the trust.
Charles, left, meets John as he arrives for the Royal Variety Performance at the Royal Albert Hall in London, on Nov. 22, 2024. (Toby Melville/Reuters)
Charles and John shared memories of performances by musicians in support of the charity's initiatives — from rock galas at Wembley Arena to concerts in Hyde Park.
"If ⁠you champion a young artist and show you believe in them, it makes all the difference," John said. "Young people are ​our future."
Vovk saw little precedent for Charles sitting down across the table from John.
"It's potentially groundbreaking. I think this is the first time that the sovereign has done something that would be classified in this way as entertainment," he said.

"To actually sit down and have a recorded conversation with the sovereign is extraordinarily rare. Elizabeth did a few of them in her final years, but these were all about reminiscences around the Crown jewels, coronation ceremony, her father…. To have something that is so, well, mainstream, is really unheard of."

John, second from left, Charles and Tim Cook, Apple's executive chairman, pose with mentees during a music workshop for young peopleat Battersea Power Station in southwest London, on Oct. 7. (Ben Stansall/Reuters)
Royally quotable
"I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time. This is the same in nature."
— Catherine, Princess of Wales, regarding her recovery from cancer. She made the comment in an interview in an issue of Country Life magazine that was guest-edited by her husband, Prince William.
Royal reads

Prince William has expressed his frustration at the way women are treated in the military. The future head of the British Armed Forces has been holding under-the-radar meetings with female service personnel as part of a drive to ensure they feel "safe, respected and valued." [Daily Mail]
Prince William's Duchy of Cornwall has apologized to tenants for its handling of the sale of an estate in southwestern England and promised new valuations of their farms and homes. [The Observer]
Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, told Rohingya refugees in the camps at Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh "we won't walk away" after hearing about the hardships they face. [The Independent]

Prince Harry and five other prominent figures have launched a legal challenge against a judge's verdict in their unsuccessful claims against the Daily Mail's publisher, Associated Newspapers. [The Guardian]
The Princess of Wales met with families gaining extra support for their youngsters' social development at a community hospital in southern England. [ITV]

The Prince of Wales made another European away trip in support of soccer team Aston Villa as he attended a Champions League match against Barcelona. William was joined by his son, Prince George. [ESPN]
Prince George contributed a colourful drawing of a kingfisher to the edition of Country Life guest-edited by his father. [Country Life]
Catherine, Princess of Wales, left, meets Ruby, nine months old, during a visit to the Chase Community Hospital on Wednesday in Bordon, England. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)

articles.title: AI cheating scandal rattles South Korea as annual college exam looms
articles.summary:
Fears for national entrance exam next week, as top scorer on tax exam admits sending photos of questions to AI tool

The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for…

blocks.text: The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true. On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.

The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

“I cheated using ⁠electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the top score was not ​the result of fair effort,” the candidate said, ‌identifying himself by the ‌surname Han, as he apologised on the YouTube channel Attorney Lee Don-ho.

Han, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.
Speaking on camera wearing a face mask, Han said he had submitted a written confession to Seoul police.

The Seoul metropolitan police agency said: “We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” adding that the case had been assigned to investigators.

The scandal has rattled a ‌country where standardised tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories. It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

“The presidential office views ​the matter very seriously, and because the college entrance exam is next week, we have been working hard to prepare countermeasures,” a senior presidential office official told reporters on Sunday.

The official said that reports of potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam were concerning, adding ⁠that the presidential chief of staff for policy would convene an emergency meeting later ​in the afternoon to ​address the issue.

The prime minister, Han Seong-sook, acknowledged on Friday public concerns over AI-assisted cheating. The government would “prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably”, a statement from her office said.
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this article

articles.title: Macron urges unity as Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia
articles.summary: Leaders of French-speaking nations gathered in Phnom Penh as a row over who should lead the Francophonie and Congo’s threat to quit put pressure on Macron to broker consensus.

image.caption: Cambodia is taking over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, after France served as the host nation in 2024Image: Soveit Yarn/REUTERS

blocks.text: A summit of French-speaking nations opened Sunday in Phnom Penh, with French President Emmanuel Macron trying to head off a walkout by the group's biggest African member over who will lead it next.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) brings together about 90 states and governments, including 53 full members, from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Canada.
It is made up of countries that use French as an official language, former French colonies, and other states with substantial historic ties to France.
What is the disagreement about?
The OIF is set to choose its next secretary-general on Monday.

Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who has held the post since 2018, is seeking a third term. DR Congo has threatened to leave if she is re-elected, accusing Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in eastern Congo, an accusation Rwanda denies.

DR Congo has 57.3 million French speakers, second only to France, per the OIF, so its exit would be a major blow. Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew from the association last year after their membership was suspended over coups.
On Saturday, DR Congo said it was withdrawing its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country's martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.
Kinshasa said it would back former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos to allow "consensus around a unifying candidacy."
AFP described the offer as conditional on Rwanda also stepping aside. However, Rwanda's foreign minister said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race.
What did Macron say?
Macron warned against "internal fractures" in the group.
"We must ensure that we preserve what constitutes its strength—namely, its unity," he said.
Rwanda said Macron had asked President Paul Kagame to withdraw his candidate, which it refused. Macron's office said Paris suggested both candidates step aside.

"With that intervention we're going backwards, to the idea that France decides," a member of a non-African delegation told AFP anonymously. France is the largest donor, and Canada provides 25% of the budget.
Macron arrives amid unrest at home, where more than 600,000 people marched earlier this month over wages and in support of student protests, with thousands arrested.

UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press Cambodia, which has been referred to as a de facto one-party state, to free detained activists. "No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions," he said.
Cambodia: USAID freeze imperils human rights, press freedom

articles.title: Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance
articles.summary: Events are being held for Volkstrauertag, a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts say the country is headed for a budget crisis. DW has more.

image.caption: The Neue Wache in Berlin is the central German memorial for victims of warImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 15, 2026
Germany marks day of mourning for victims of war and oppression

blocks.caption: Germany is remembering victims of war and oppressionImage: imago images/Udo Gottschalk

blocks.text: Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.
Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.
There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.
In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.
Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.
"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

articles.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary:
International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel

The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this…

blocks.text: The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

blocks.caption: The Kutupalong Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Munir Uz Zaman/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a military airstrike on a market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, a rebel-held area in western Rakhine state, 28 September 2026. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The former general is separately b​eing investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.
The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

blocks.caption: Min Aung Hlaing, president of Myanmar, speaks during a meeting with Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin in August. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/Pool AP/AP

blocks.text: However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.
More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.
A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.
“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

articles.title: How AI is likely to change Germany's job market
articles.summary: The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists are not convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask…

image.caption: Artificial Intelligence is predicted to cost hundreds of thousands of jobs in Germany aloneImage: Tobias Schwarz/AFP

blocks.text: At the German government's 2026 "Digital Summit" in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July this year, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring last year, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
The impending job rupture

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world. This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socio-economic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."
How AI is changing the working world
Why tech bosses love UBI

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the non-profit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of UBI.

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income (UBI) is very old: The English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances that they said AI would bring. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable.

Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

But Herrmann says it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She is not convinced that organizations like hers and people like Elon Musk want the same thing. "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."
Is AI killing creative jobs?

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at Oxford University and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he told DW by email. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"
Work-life integration: A new ideal?

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history: Partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact: AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socio-economic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she puts it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argues, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work: "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," Herrmann said. "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

articles.title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.summary:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings

The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this…

blocks.text: The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.

Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Manila on Friday object to Donald Trump’s participation in the Asean summit. Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPA

blocks.text: Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.

“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”

Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines, starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.

blocks.caption: A poster in Siem Reap on Friday shows Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte, flanking Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihamoni, as the capital prepares for the Francophone summit. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.

Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea, where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.

The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.

blocks.caption: Passengers arrive at Shenzhen airport ahead of the Apec summit.   Photograph: Ng Han Guan/AP

blocks.text: Global pivots towards Asia

For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.

Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.

Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.

“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Manila make their feelings known before the arrival of Donald Trump for the Asean meeting.  Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPA

blocks.text: Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.

Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas. Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.

A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore.

Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration. Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.
Additional research by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Tens of thousands continue to protest across France
articles.summary: Some 106,000 people marched through French cities for a fifth consecutive weekend of protests, marking the lowest turnout in recent weeks.

image.caption: Protests that began over underfunded schools have since spread to wider public grievancesImage: Benoit Tessier/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday to demonstrate against the rising cost of living and strained public services, the Interior Ministry said.

Saturday's demonstrations drew their lowest turnout in recent weeks. Some 106,000 people marched through French cities, with 24,000 in Paris alone. The previous weekend, some 146,000 people had participated nationwide.
The number of arrests was also significantly lower. Police detained 219 people across the country, according to the Interior Ministry.
Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful, police fired tear gas in Paris, Bordeaux and the western city of Nantes, including after some protesters shot fireworks.
French business owners share harrowing accounts of violent protests
France's protests expose deeper anger
Mass protests have swept across the European Union's second-largest economy for more than a month.

What began in September as student protests against teacher shortages and poor facilities has since evolved into a broader movement fuelled by anger over the rising cost of living, strained public services and police brutality.
In mid-October, around 565,000 people took to the streets across France, as riots, looting and clashes disrupted demonstrations in several cities.
As France entered its fifth consecutive weekend of nationwide unrest, President Emmanuel Macron's approval ratings fell to the lowest level since he took office in 2017, according to recent polls.
The French government doesn't have much room to respond to the protesters' demands due to its high debt.
Could France's debt crisis become a problem for Europe?

articles.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
articles.summary: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.

blocks.text: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
Image source, Braton Serge/BBC
ByRuth Alonga
BBC AfricaReporting fromButembo

When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is real

blocks.text: Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is real
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about Ebola

blocks.text: Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about Ebola
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

blocks.caption: Graphic showing how Ebola attacks the human body, sourced to the WHO and Cleveland Clinic. Graphic showing how Ebola systematically attacks the human body. It explains that symptoms appear two to 21 days after contact and can worsen over time. Earlier symptoms, shown with purple circles around di…

blocks.text: Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."
BBC Africa podcasts

articles.title: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
articles.summary: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletes
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.
That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram alone

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram alone
Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.
So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?
"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.
"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.
But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next president

blocks.text: Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next president

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.
Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.
All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.
"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."
It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.
But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?
In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services

blocks.text: Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.
In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.
The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.
The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to run

blocks.text: Image source, Pool/AFP via Getty Images
President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to run
The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.
So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.
Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.
In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".
If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.
In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

articles.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
articles.summary: SpaceX has performed the historic catch using mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".

blocks.text: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.
"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:27 local time (21:27 GMT) on Saturday and was successfuly caught.

articles.title: Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt
articles.summary: The 2027 federal budget proposal has finally been hammered out and is set for a vote in parliament. What are the government's policy priorities in defense, infrastructure, the economy and social…

image.caption: Lawmakers worked through the night to hammer out the details of the federal budgetImage: Carsten Koall/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday morning when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session. Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion). But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.
Germanys slow road to recovery

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party spoke of a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
Why is debt growing? Crises drive up costs

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities a government and a country set — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.
What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.
Defense spending continues to rise

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June 2026, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.
How risky is the German government's borrowing spree?
The largest item in the budget: social spending and pensions

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise. People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than one million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.
The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.
Germany is no longer a model of fiscal discipline

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.
German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses
Economic experts warn of rising debt
The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.
German Chancellor Merz vows to push ahead with reforms
The road ahead

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during his visit to Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."

articles.title: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia
articles.summary:
Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok

Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’…

blocks.text: Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.
